summary: This informational document supports work analyzing routing protocol authentication per RFC 6518. It builds an operational and management model for routing protocol security that works across protocols.

eli5.summary: Routing devices need locks on their conversations. This sets out how administrators should run and manage those locks.

questions: how to manage routing protocol keys
subtitle: Guidelines for managing router authentication keys in networks

tldr.problem: As routing protocols adopt cryptographic authentication, network operators need practical guidance on how to manage, deploy, and operate authentication keys across routers without disrupting network connectivity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides an operational and management model covering key table configuration, credential types (preshared keys and public keys), peer grouping, enrollment procedures, and fault handling.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can deploy routing protocol authentication reliably by following these recommendations, and protocol designers can build systems that work in real operational environments.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Operational model for routing protocol security

today: RFC 7211 is an Informational RFC that provides guidance for operators implementing KARP. The key table mechanism (RFC 7210) has been adopted in routing protocol standards. The operational guidance remains relevant as network operators gradually move from manual key management to automated systems.

sections.title: Routing Protocol Authentication and KARP
sections.content:
The Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols (KARP) working group is designing improvements to how routing protocols authenticate each other. Routing protocols like OSPF, IS-IS, and BGP need to verify that routing information comes from legitimate neighbors, not attackers. Historically, this was done with simple preshared keys. The KARP effort aims to improve both the cryptographic mechanisms and the key management system.

However, deploying authentication securely across a real network requires more than just choosing a good cryptographic algorithm. Network operators need clear guidance on how to configure routers, manage keys across multiple devices, handle key expiration and rotation, deal with router failures, and gradually upgrade networks from manual key management to automated key management. This document provides that guidance, helping establish a common baseline for management capabilities across different vendors and protocols.
sections.eli5: Routing protocols need keys so they can prove to each other that they're real routers and not hackers. But keys need to be stored, rotated, and managed across hundreds of routers. This document is a how-to guide for operators.

sections.title: Key Configuration and Management
sections.content:
Routing keys are stored in a key table that holds both the key material and parameters for using it. The key table is separate from the routing protocol configuration, allowing keys to be managed independently. Different routing protocols have different scope requirements: some use per-peer keys, some use per-interface keys, some use area-wide keys. For example, OSPF typically uses the same key on all routers on a link, but different keys for different links.

Good key management should support inheritance of default configurations at broader scopes with per-interface overrides, to prevent keys on different links from becoming out-of-sync. The key table must validate that keys are appropriate for their protocol (correct algorithms, correct directions, valid derivation functions). Additionally, management interfaces should provide an easy mechanism to update key expiration times, transition keys from receive-only to send-enabled, and enable or disable keys. Some operational models allow using an expired key to keep existing security associations alive if no new key is available; others require associations to fail. Both approaches should be supported.
sections.eli5: A key table is like a spreadsheet listing all the keys, which router they go with, when they expire, and whether they're currently being used. Good management tools let operators update a key's expiration date or turn it on and off without breaking the network.

sections.title: Authentication Methods: Preshared Keys and Public Keys
sections.content:
The document covers multiple authentication approaches. Preshared keys, the simplest method, are keys known by a group of routers. They authenticate that a message sender knows the key, but do not cryptographically identify which specific peer sent it; instead, identity is inferred from routing protocol trust rules. Preshared keys can be used directly as traffic keys, or fed into a key derivation function (KDF) to generate fresh session keys that combine the preshared key with session-specific values.

Public keys offer alternatives. The simplest is hashing the public key and storing the hash in each router, avoiding the need for a full Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) but requiring all routers to be updated when peers' keys change. A full PKI using certificates offers more scalability but introduces operational complexity around certification practices, revocation, and validation. The document notes that self-signed certificates can bridge these approaches.

A critical consideration is key separation: using the same key in multiple protocols can create cross-protocol attacks where a message valid in one protocol is misinterpreted by another. Operators must be aware of this risk, and protocol designers should use key derivation to ensure different protocols produce different cryptographic keys even from the same input key.
sections.eli5: Preshared keys are simple: a password that two routers know. Public keys are harder to set up but work better at scale. The catch: never use the same key for two different protocols, or attackers might exploit that.

sections.title: Operational Challenges: Enrollment, Faults, and Grouping
sections.content:
When deploying new routers, operators must configure keying material. The document recommends treating this like any other router configuration (passwords, AAA secrets), using existing procedures. Higher-assurance procedures (like generating private keys on a router and never exporting them) are possible but not mandatory for initial deployment.

Grouping peers correctly is essential. The document identifies complex relationships: a peer may have multiple keys during transitions; a key may apply to multiple peers in group authentication; peers may be auto-discovered (as on broadcast links) or explicitly configured. Management interfaces should support attaching authorization information to peer configuration objects, grouping peers for shared keys, and expressing trust boundaries (e.g., different keys for different sides of a trust boundary in BGP).

Fault handling requires proactive monitoring and notifications. Implementations should notify operators before keys expire (via console messages, logs, SNMP traps, or protocol messages). When hardware fails, operators typically restore minimal configuration to reach management servers; keys should be recoverable centrally so a replacement router can quickly resume operation. Alternatively, if keys are never exported from routers, hardware failure requires updating peers' configurations.
sections.eli5: When you add a new router, you give it keys the same way you give it a password. When a key is about to expire, the router should warn you. When hardware fails, you need a backup of the keys or all routers need to update.

sections.title: Upgrading from Manual to Automated Key Management
sections.content:
A critical operational challenge is deploying automated key management without disrupting existing routing. This requires a phased approach. For peer-to-peer protocols like BGP, the upgrade is relatively straightforward: load code supporting automated key management on both peers, then configure the adjacency to use the automated system.

For multicast protocols like OSPF and IS-IS, the challenge is greater. Bringing down an entire link to reconfigure it is undesirable. Two approaches are recommended: First, support running both manual and automated keying on the same link simultaneously, allowing a transition period. Second, have the automated key management protocol export the current manual group key through the new system, so all nodes use the same key initially, then generate a new fresh key only after all nodes have transitioned to automated management. Group key management protocols are recommended to support exporting existing manual keys during initial deployment.

The document emphasizes that even with technical mechanisms for zero-disruption upgrades, operational practices must be carefully designed. Today, many operators do not rotate keys because the perceived cost of an update is higher than the risk of compromise. Deployment that works with existing operational practices is more likely to be adopted than deployment requiring new procedures.
sections.eli5: Moving from manual to automated keys is risky. For two-router connections, it's easy: upgrade both and switch over. For big networks, you need to run both systems at once during the switch, so nothing breaks.
